title: Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length from that position, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first.
shortTitle: Jump Game: can you reach the last index (greedy reachability)
keyPoints: Maintain a single farthest-reach variable starting at zero and scan the array left to right.
If the current index exceeds the farthest reach, the last index is unreachable and we return false.
At each reachable index, update the farthest reach to the maximum of itself and the index plus its jump value.
Reachability is monotone and contiguous from zero, so one integer captures the entire reachable set.
The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, replacing an O(n squared) DP solution.
Early termination when the farthest reach covers the last index avoids unnecessary iterations.

s1_definition.oneliner: Track farthest reach; if i > reach you are stuck; else extend reach.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Jump Game** – a reachability problem where each array element represents the maximum jump length from that position, and we determine whether the last index is reachable from index zero.
- **Greedy frontier** – maintain a single integer `reach` starting at zero, updated as `max(reach, i + nums[i])` at each step.
- **Stuck condition** – if the current index `i` exceeds `reach`, no earlier position could have jumped here, so we return `false`.
- **Monotone property** – reachability is contiguous from zero, so the entire reachable set collapses to one number.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time for a single pass and O(1) space for one variable.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a settlement pipeline has stages, and each stage declares how many stages ahead it can skip based on its clearing capacity. Rajesh walks the pipeline tracking the farthest stage reachable so far. If he ever stands beyond that frontier, the pipeline cannot complete.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Array:   [2]  [3]  [1]  [1]  [4]
Index:    0    1    2    3    4

Scan left to right:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ i=0: reach = max(0, 0+2) = 2           │
│      Reachable: [0────2]               │
│ i=1: 1 <= 2 ✓  reach = max(2, 1+3) = 4 │
│      Reachable: [0────────────4]        │
│      4 >= 4 (last index) → return true  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Failing:  [3]  [2]  [1]  [0]  [4]
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ i=0: reach=3   i=1: reach=3            │
│ i=2: reach=3   i=3: reach=3            │
│ i=4: 4 > 3 → STUCK → return false      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Forward greedy vs Backward greedy:
  Forward:  track farthest reachable from left
  Backward: track last good position from right
  Both: O(n) time, O(1) space
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game is a greedy reachability problem. I keep a single variable for the farthest index I can reach so far and walk the array left to right. At each index, if the index is already beyond my farthest reach, I could never have arrived there and I return false. Otherwise I extend the reach to the maximum of its current value and the index plus the jump available there.

The greedy is correct because reachability is monotone: if I can reach some index, I can reach everything up to my current frontier, so I never need to know which exact path got me there, only the single farthest point. If the walk completes without getting stranded, the last index is reachable. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, collapsing the quadratic DP into a single integer.

Edge cases include a single-element array (trivially true), an array starting with zero (immediate failure if length is greater than one), and arrays where the first element covers the entire range. The common mistake is updating the reach without first checking whether the current index is reachable.

At the National Bank of India, a settlement pipeline had stages where each stage declared how many stages ahead it could skip, and operations needed to know if the final stage was reachable from the start. The constant-space greedy frontier gave the answer in a single pass.

Remember one sentence: track the farthest reachable index, and if you ever stand beyond it, you are stuck.
